notes: Near Atlanta, Ga. Received letters of July 17th and 18th. Surprised to hear 153rd was in Maryland — knew Gen'l. Canby's troops there, didn't suppose 153rd among them. **HEAVY CANNONADE — extreme left.** 23rd Corps (Gen'l. Schofield) moving to right. Object: **STRIKE MACON AND ATLANTA RAILROAD.** Lines within half mile of road. Sunday night constructing new line of work — obliged to work at night on account of rebel sharpshooters. **SHARPSHOOTER HIT THE MAIL** — ball "spot" into center of crowd collecting mail; passed through tent. "It made them jump a little but they did not scatter until they had got their letters." James and Charles haven't written — "Why does not James write!" Feels neglected. "I would do almost anything for him."
transcription:
Aug. 2, 1864
Near Atlanta, Ga.

Dear Mother:

I received your letter of July 17th and 18th a day or two since and was pleased to hear that you are all well and considerably surprised to hear the 153d was in Maryland. I knew that Gen'l. Canby's troops were there, but did not suppose that the 153d was among them.

Quite a heavy cannonade has been going on today to the extreme left of the line. The 23d Corps (Gen'l. Schofield) was moving to the right yesterday and the day before. I suppose it is them engaged. The distance is so great that I cannot tell whether or not it is accompanied with musketry. The object of the move is, I think, to strike out the Macon and Atlanta railroad. Our lines, I understand, were within a half mile of the road previous to the 23d Corps going there.

Nothing of special interest has transpired since last I wrote you. Sunday night we commenced constructing a new line of work. We were obliged to work in the night on account of the rebel sharpshooters. They plunged two or three balls into the works the next day but did no damage. Last night while the mail was being distributed (a large crowd always collects around the mail) a rebel sharpshooter, I should think nearly a mile away, sent a ball "spot" into the center of the circle. It made them jump a little but they did not scatter until they had got their letters. The ball passed through a tent in its course. The mail carrier is collecting the mail. I must hurry. I want to write James and Charles, but will not until I learn surely whether they are in Maryland. Why does not James write! I feel quite neglected. There surely cannot be one who has a heartier interest in his welfare than I. I would do almost anything for him. Remember me to Charles and James when you next write, and ask them why they do not write me. Please write often. I have — Love to all.

Your aff. son,

Alexander.
editorial:
The sharpshooter hitting the mail call is one of the collection's most vivid siege details. A ball from nearly a mile away, "spot" into the center of the crowd — and "they did not scatter until they had got their letters." Mail was more important than safety. The ball passed through a tent on its way. Alexander is writing while the mail carrier collects outgoing letters — the same mail system that just survived a sniper shot.

The flanking movement toward the Macon & Atlanta railroad is Sherman's endgame strategy: cut every railroad feeding Atlanta and the city must fall. The 23rd Corps (Schofield) joins the 15th, 16th, and 17th in the rightward sweep. Lines within half a mile of the railroad.

"Why does not James write!" — the youngest brother's silence hurts. "I would do almost anything for him." Alexander, under daily fire outside Atlanta, worries about his teenage brother's feelings more than his own safety.

transcription:
[At the top of the letter was written: "My dearest child; Write me immediately."]

Aug. 8, 1864
Near Atlanta, Ga.

Dear Mother:

I received your letter of July 25th day before yesterday and your papers, the "Times" and the "Tribune" the day before, also the envelopes and paper enclosed. As I had written you the day I thought I had fulfilled your request of writing you immediately, but like a dutiful son I shall write you again today. Now, "ain't" I a good boy?

You recollect when I last wrote that I mentioned that the armies of McPherson and Schofield were moving to the right. Since then a battle has come off in which our forces were victorious, driving the enemy a mile and a half — taking a fort and a battery, and cutting, I understand, the only remaining road of the rebels. But then I will not weary you with a detailed account of this affair, as you will have seen accounts of it in the papers long before this reaches you.

I regret to inform you that Gen'l. Hooker has left us. He had endeared himself to the whole corps. The day he left he rode along the line bidding the men goodbye. A man from one of the Pennsylvania regts. of our brigade had just had his leg taken off by a cannon shot, was being carried off on a stretcher just at that time. "Good bye, General Hooker!" he sang out. It seemed to have moved the Gen'l. greatly. He got off his horse, took off his hat and went up and shook hands with the poor fellow, making some kind encouraging words at the same time. The 20th Corps will never forget old "Fighting Joe." Major Gen'l. Slocum, our old Corps commander, is now I understand in command of the Corps. We feel somewhat comforted for the loss of Hooker.

I suppose Charles and James are now on the Peninsula with Grant, as the excitement occasioned by the last raid must be nearly over. I hope the report of Charles being ill is not true, but if it is he is where he can get the best medical treatment. I shall try and write them both today. I hope James will try and bear his disappointment like a man. I am afraid it is he instead of Charles that is ill. I suppose Frances is still enjoying her visit at C. Have been expecting a letter from her for some time. She will write soon. I have not a solitary stamp and hardly know what I shall do to end this letter. If you can do so without inconveniencing yourself, please send me some in your next letter. I do not think I have received all the stamps you have sent. I have not received the tea as yet. Culver Bostwick received some some time since. Please write often. Love to all. Give my regards to Mrs. Brikerhoff.

Your aff. Son,

Alex F. Hubbell
editorial:
Hooker's farewell is the most cinematic scene Alexander has written — the general riding along the line, the legless Pennsylvania soldier calling out from his stretcher "Good bye, General Hooker!", Hooker dismounting, removing his hat, shaking the man's hand. "It seemed to have moved the Gen'l. greatly." The 20th Corps loved Hooker, and Hooker loved them back. His departure was a command dispute — passed over for the Army of the Tennessee after McPherson's death on July 22 — but to the men it was a loss beyond measure. "The 20th Corps will never forget old 'Fighting Joe.'"

The battle on the right — driving the enemy a mile and a half, taking a fort and battery, cutting "the only remaining road" — is the Ezra Church/Utoy Creek fighting of late July. Sherman's flanking strategy is working. The roads feeding Atlanta are being severed one by one.

"My dearest child; Write me immediately" — written at the top of the letter, likely by Alexander's mother on receipt, or possibly Alexander's own urgent appeal. "Now, 'ain't' I a good boy?" — the playful tone of a man who writes faithfully even when he has no stamps.
sigSummary: Hooker leaves the 20th Corps near Atlanta, and Alexander captures the scene that broke the men's hearts: a Pennsylvania soldier, his leg just shot off by a cannon, calls from the stretcher, "Good bye, General Hooker!" The general dismounts, removes his hat, and shakes the dying man's hand. On the right, fighting drives the enemy a mile and a half, taking a fort and battery and cutting "the only remaining road of the rebels." And still, no stamps: "ain't I a good boy?"

SAVED TWO DIVISION BATTERIES.** Rebs had use of Bundy's battery guns. 60th only regiment not broken during fight. At Lost Mountain — 60th only regt. to reach top. Capt. transcription:
August 8th, 1864

Capt. J. M. Ransom —

Dear Sir:

I received your kind letter of July 10th some days since, but knowing as you do how we soldiers are situated on an active campaign, I trust you will excuse my tardiness in answering. My Mother was right in telling you that I would be very much pleased by the receipt of a letter from you. I was indeed pleased — and sincerely trust they will be less like "angel's visits" in the future.

I have so much to write that I hardly know where to begin — and for that very reason had a good will not to begin at all — but nevertheless I will do my best. Everything seems to be going on here most favorably. The theatre of the most active operations for the last few days has been the extreme right. I will not weary you with a detailed account of its late movements as you will have seen a full acct. of them in the papers long before this reaches you. Suffice it to say that the combined attack of the forces of Howard, (formerly McPherson's) and Schofield was very successful, and that the last remaining railroad to the rebs is severed. I hope we shall be able to bag the Johnnies here, for I am heartily tired of chasing them.

They are bringing us, I understand, a heavy siege train — so I expect the Johnnies are in a pretty tight place. The hardest fighting of the campaign has occurred since we crossed the Chattahoochee and all the Johnnies have to show for it is a long list of casualties that would frighten a man just to look at it. How comforting such a document must be to Jeff Davis & Co. The fight of the 20th of July was an awful one. The rebels threw their men upon us in solid columns and seemed bound to drive us into the Chattahoochee. But we were not to be driven. We had come all the way from Chattanooga to see Atlanta and were bound to see it and are now knocking pretty loudly at its doors.

We changed front during the battle no less than three times. I thought matters looked a little "scaly" when I saw the rebs coming up in our rear, but for all that we whipped them. Our regt. and the 147th Penn. have the credit of saving the two Division batteries. The rebs had the use of the guns of Bundy's battery when we came up. Our regt. was the only one of the Brigade that was not broken during the fight. At the fight at Lost Mountain our regt. was the only one of the Brig. that got up to the top of the hill and held the ground. Capt. Delaney was wounded in the fight of the 20th. I have reached nearly the end of my sheets and have not said half what I wish to say. Shall have to leave it to another letter.

Yours truly,

Alex F. Hubbell.

P. H. Brookway has got a commission and is in command of Co. H. Capt. Elliott is now Major and Thomas is Lieut./Col., Goddard is Colonel. We are to be consolidated soon with the 134th N.Y. Hobart is Capt. of Co. I. A good many of the officers will be mustered out when we are consolidated. The surplus non coms are to be reduced. P. H. Brookway has a first Lieut. commission.
editorial:
This letter to Capt. Ransom is Alexander's most detailed battle account. Writing to a fellow officer rather than his mother, Alexander gives the Peachtree Creek narrative he couldn't write home: "The rebels threw their men upon us in solid columns and seemed bound to drive us into the Chattahoochee. But we were not to be driven. We had come all the way from Chattanooga to see Atlanta and were bound to see it." The pride is earned — the 60th was the only regiment not broken during the fight.

"I thought matters looked a little 'scaly' when I saw the rebs coming up in our rear" — the understatement of a man who saw his regiment nearly flanked and overrun. Changing front three times during a battle means the regiment was nearly surrounded and had to fight in multiple directions.

The consolidation with the 134th N.Y. is ominous for Alexander: "surplus non coms are to be reduced." As a sergeant, his rank is at risk. The army's organizational efficiency collides with individual soldiers' careers.

"I have reached nearly the end of my sheets and have not said half what I wish to say." — the frustration of a natural writer who has too much war to describe and too little paper to describe it on.

author: james
notes: Baltimore, Md. (Frederick City hospital). Long while since written — last letter from Morganza. Left Louisiana last of June for North. **EARLY'S RAID — WASHINGTON DEFENSES.** Placed in rifle pits; heavy skirmishing; rebs retreated. Sent as reserve for 6th Corps — followed rebs to Shenandoah Valley. 6th Corps skirmishing but Johnnies did not want to fight. Crossed river, lay in belt of woods expecting fight — enemy only wanted to get off with plunder. Ordered to report Washington within 24 hours. **NIGHT MARCH — EXHAUSTION.** Four men came in with dressed porker. Pig hitting briskly that afternoon. **HARDTACK DESCRIBED** — "Bake a flour and water cake with no salt or saleratus on a griddle till it is hard." Waded river, marched until four next day. **FELL OUT** — blistered foot, fatigue, want of sleep. Wagon train. Chainbridge. Shoes and clothes issued. Marched to Harper's Ferry, then counter march. **FREDERICK CITY HOSPITAL** — two weeks. "My sickness was generally unwell and played out." Hospital on hill overlooking city. Milk 16¢/qt, peaches 80¢/bu. **INDIGNATION ABOUT EARLY'S RAID** — 20,000 troops around Washington (veterans), rebel force only 15,000. Army came up, harvested, plundered, got off with wagon train three miles long. **CHARLIE'S HEALTH** — thin and used up, finds marches hard. "Charlie is one of the kind that'll go until he cannot go." Soft bread, pilot bread, meat twice a day, stewed apples.
transcription:
Aug. 15th, 1864
Baltimore, Md.

Dear Mother and Fannie:

It is a long while since I have written you. I think my last letter was from Morganza. Since that time our regt. has seen considerable hardship. We left Louisiana the last of June for the North — this, I think Charlie has written you. As soon as we arrived at Washington D.C. we were sent out to the defenses and placed in the rifle pits. The next morning there was heavy skirmishing near us, but the Rebs retreated and we saw nothing of them. The next day we were sent as a reserve for the 6th Corps and followed the Rebs out to the Shenandoah Valley, the 6th Corps following close and skirmishing, but the Johnnies did not want to fight. We crossed a day and the next we crossed the river and lay in a belt of woods all day expecting a fight, but no, the enemy only wanted to get off with their plunder and keep us off, and they did it. At night we received orders to report at Washington within 24 hours. "Fall in!" ran along the lines and off we marched, many with light eyes and gloomy feelings — the prospect of marching all night does not lighten the feelings of many. Just as we were starting four men came in with a large dressed porker but it was goodly big, for a soldier cannot carry more than his usual load. Pig hitting had gone on pretty briskly that afternoon. Some were fortunate enough to get their pork for supper. Hardtack and coffee was all most of us had to eat. Do you know what hardtack is! Bake a flour and water cake with no salt or saleratus on a griddle till it is hard — throw it on a shelf for three or four days and see what kind of a meal it will make.

We waded the river and with an occasional half hour rest marched until four the next day. I stood it until about eight the next morning and then the want of sleep and food, a blistered foot and fatigue compelled me to fall out. The wagon train soon came along. I put my gun and bundles on one and found I could get along. I kept with this train until we arrived at Chainbridge within the defenses of W. There we consumed. Orders were soon issued to prepare for field service; shoes and clothes were given out, and after a day's rest off we started. Where we went I did not know or care. After several days hard marching the two corps pitched camp about two miles beyond Harper's Ferry. Then came a counter march. Our Generals marched and counter-marched without seeming to come to any determination, the men in the meantime becoming worn out. At Frederick City I was taken to a hospital where I am now and have been two weeks. I was quite sick but am now pretty well and expect soon to go to a convalescent camp. My sickness was generally unwell and played out. The hospital is pleasantly situated on a hill overlooking the city. Papers are brought in every morning with war and city news. They do not apprehend a draft here — the wards are fast filling out their quotas. Milk is retailed at 16 cents a quart; peaches are selling at 80 cents a bushel. I had a little change and could buy fruit. We get tea four a cent here.

There is a general feeling indignation expressed in these papers that our Generals should not have ascertained the actual force of the enemy and prevented them from coming so near our Capitol. They state that we had twenty thousand troops around Washington, part of them veterans, while the actual forces of the Rebels was 15,000, since ascertained. The fact that the army came up here with that force, harvested, plundered and got off with a wagon train three miles in length is rather irritating to us.

About Charlie's health — he was quite thin and used up when I left; he finds the marches very hard. Charlie is one of the kind that'll go until he cannot go. I do not think that is the way. He remarked that if he was sick he would not have vital energy enough to recover. A good rest and something to eat would set him all right, I think. I hope he has been sent off. Charlie is pretty plucky and won't give up, but I think he ought to favor himself more.

This paper was given me when we arrived at Washington from Louisiana. This I have carried since then which accounts for its being soiled. Our fare here is soft bread or pilot bread, meat twice a day, stewed apples at night.

It seems to me that I should like to come up with the Johnnies and have a good hard fight with them instead of dogging them day and night and then having them get away marching and countermarching, accomplishing nothing, I do not like. What is the news in C? Will they be obliged to draft them in Sept.? Please write soon. Direct as before.

James
editorial:
James's account of Early's Raid is the youngest brother's first real combat narrative — and it's a story of frustration, not glory. Sent from the heat of Louisiana to the defenses of Washington, placed in rifle pits, sent to chase Early through the Shenandoah Valley — and the rebels escaped with a three-mile wagon train of plunder. "Our Generals marched and counter-marched without seeming to come to any determination." The indignation is shared by the newspapers and the soldiers alike.

The hardtack definition is priceless — written for Mother and Frances who have never seen one: "Bake a flour and water cake with no salt or saleratus on a griddle till it is hard — throw it on a shelf for three or four days and see what kind of a meal it will make." The doughnut-maker of Morganza (LTR-1864-06-29-001) has graduated to hardtack.

"My sickness was generally unwell and played out" — James's laconic diagnosis. He was exhausted. The army wore him out with marching and counter-marching, and his body gave up at Frederick City. The hospital on the hill with its peaches and milk is a world away from the Shenandoah pursuit.
sigSummary: Frederick City's hospital sits pleasantly on a hill overlooking the city, but young James writes Mother and Fannie of frustration, not glory: sent from Louisiana to Washington's defenses, dropped into rifle pits, then chasing Early through the Shenandoah while the rebels escaped with a plundered wagon train three miles long. "Our Generals marched and counter-marched without seeming to come to any determination," he writes — until a blistered foot and want of sleep dropped him from the column.

transcription:
Aug. 22, 1864
2d Div. Hospital — 20th Corps
Near Atlanta, Ga.

Dear Mother:

You perceive that I am again in the hospital. I am not wounded but am afflicted with what the surgeon calls genuine scurvy. He says I am very young to have it. By taking good care of myself and with proper nourishment (vegetables) I think I shall soon be fit for duty.

I received your letter of August 8th yesterday. Dixon brought it down to me. You may be sure I was pleased for I had not heard from you since the 25th of July. I have received several papers since then. You did not send me a Tribune with an acct. of the battle of the 20th. I should like to see it. If you can, please send it or any other paper with an acct. of it.

Nothing of special interest has transpired since I last wrote — yes, there has too, if the report is true. Very heavy artillery and musketry firing was heard a day or two since to the right of the line and the report of the affair is that a heavy battle came off there, the rebels charging and recharging our works, but were repulsed each time with terrible slaughter. Their loss, it is said, is to be counted by the thousand. The rebels are reported to have been very much under the influence of liquor. Reports are so conflicting that I hardly dare write them. Of a battle having taken place I have but little doubt as the firing was very sharp. You must bear in mind that our line is many miles long and we can only judge what is going on by the firing. There are so many rumors afloat that you can hardly tell what is reliable till you see the papers.

Please send papers often and a magazine now and then if convenient. Please write soon and often. Lieut. Brookway has taken charge of my mail and will forward it to me wherever I am. Please send me some stamps. I will use my last when I send this. I found the two stamps I lost. Mrs Frances yet returned? Tell her I received her letter and didn't see my boots for a week after. I will endeavor to write to her soon. I wrote James and Charles a few days since. I hope that they will write me. I think your fears are groundless about their being prisoners. Love to all. F. A. Cook is at Champlain, and he is hot for Lincoln. I will hoist my colors soon. If I live I shall cast a vote this fall. You know I will have been in the service over three years when the election comes off, and according to the laws of the U.S. I shall be of proper age to vote, as no one is received into the U.S. Service under 18. By the muster rolls I shall be over 21.

Your aff. Son

Alex F. Hubbell
editorial:
Alexander has scurvy — the disease of the age of sail, now the disease of the Atlanta Campaign. Three months of hardtack, salt pork, and no vegetables. "The surgeon says I am very young to have it." The campaign that ground him "bully thin" has now put him in the hospital.

The battle he hears from the hospital — rebs charging, repulsed with terrible slaughter, drunk on liquor — is likely the Battle of Jonesborough or related fighting in late August. Alexander can only hear it: "our line is many miles long and we can only judge what is going on by the firing."

"I will hoist my colors soon" — the McClellan man is shifting. The war has changed Alexander's politics. F.A. Cook from Champlain is "hot for Lincoln," and Alexander, who yearned for McClellan four months ago, is coming around. The voting age calculation is revealing: he enlisted under 18 but will be "over 21" by the muster rolls. The army made him a man, and now it will let him vote.

transcription:
Aug. 26, 1864
Camp near Harper's Ferry

Dear Mother:

I received a letter from you last night dated Aug. 20th, was glad to hear from you, but am very sorry you are so anxious about James and me. James, I think, is all right. When around for a couple of days near Frederick James was sent to the hospital at that place, and Dr. Sweeney told me that he would send me as soon as he could but would not at that time very well. James was thin in flesh and had the diarrhea. If he has been very sick since then the doctors have made him so with their medicine. But I think James is having a good time in some hospital or convalescent camp — that is, a good time compared with marching. I have not heard from James nor have I written him. It is useless to be anxious about him because he has not written. You know, he doesn't seem to care about letter writing. Perhaps he is waiting till he rejoins the regt. As for myself I am well and have been nearly two weeks in the convalescent dept. As there are more clerks here than are necessary I may go back to the regt. any day, and then I may not. There is a good deal of work to do but then we live well. I have flatted in considerably since I have been here because I eat all the sugar I want, for one thing. You have been sending me recipes for the diarrhea, because I suppose as it is an army complaint you think I must have it. I have been troubled very little with it. I know a man with whom it has become chronic, who is a perfect skeleton. He has a good appetite and does duty all the time.

I am sorry you wasted $5 telegraphing about James. Dr. Sweeney told me at the time James was sent to the hospital that he would be sent on to Washington probably, and as I did not know his address I have not written him. James had no chevrons on his coat and I guess in his paper for admission to the Hospital Corporal was not written. I hope you will not worry about us boys, for if there is anything the matter with us you will hear of it. You must call no news good news. I am entirely out of money and postage stamps. When you would send me a couple of dollars and some stamps. You direct the letters me right. I have recd 2 or 3 letters lately from you, also two newspapers. Have not written because I have not had the material or time. We have been on the move nearly all the time, have been here two days. Our Army is composed of the 19th and the 6th Corps — also the 8th — all under the command of General Sheridan who has a large force of cavalry with him. We have not had a sight of the rebs yet, although the cavalry has fought with them some; also a few of the infantry. Please write often. It is not convenient for me to write as I have no place to carry writing materials and not much time, but I will write as often as I can. Give my love to Frances. Also don't forget yourself.

From your aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell
editorial:
Charles is in the convalescent department as a clerk, "flatted in considerably" on sugar and good food, while James is in a hospital at Frederick with diarrhea. Mother has spent $5 on a telegram about James — a significant sum — and Charles reassures her it was wasted. "Call no news good news."

Sheridan's army is forming around Harper's Ferry — the 19th, 6th, and 8th Corps with cavalry. The Shenandoah Valley campaign that will produce Third Winchester, Fisher's Hill, and Cedar Creek is about to begin. Charles and James are in it. Alexander is in a hospital near Atlanta with scurvy. Three brothers, three theaters, three hospitals.

Safe in the convalescent department as a clerk, he has "flatted in considerably" on all the sugar he can eat. His counsel is hard-won: "You must call no news good news."

notes: 2d Div. Hospital, 20th A.C. Now in hospital — will endeavor to be very regular in correspondence. Getting along as well as can be expected — scurvy will take some time. "I have very good care taken of me." Received letter Aug 16th — very sorry to hear James is sick in hospital and Charley likely to be soon. "I had a hearty laugh when I took in the idea of your three hopeful sons being in the hospital at the one and same time." Agrees not something to laugh at — "low diet and doctor's medicines are not quite as agreeable as some things." **CORPS FALLEN BACK FROM ATLANTA** — holding line along Chattahoochee. Rest of army gone on grand flanking excursion, heading toward Macon. **REPORTED REBS HAVE LEFT ATLANTA AND GONE AFTER SHERMAN.** Stirring things will happen. **SLOCUM NOW COMMANDS 6TH CORPS** [sic — should be 20th]. 1st Lieut. P. H. Brookway (formerly Orderly Sergt. of Co. H.) now commands Co. Capt. Delaney at home. Chronic diarrhea will not get hold of James and Charles. "It is a terrible disease."
transcription:
Aug. 30/64
2d Div. Hospital, 20th A.C.

Dear Mother:

Now that I am in a hospital I know you will be anxious to hear from me often and consequently I shall endeavor to be very regular in my correspondence. I am getting along as well as can be expected, though I expect will take some little time to get this scurvy out of my blood. I have very good care taken of me so you need not be troubled on that score.

I received your letter of Aug 16th day before yesterday and am glad to hear that you at home are well, and very, very sorry to hear that James is sick in hospital and Charley likely to be soon. Please excuse me, Mother, but I did have a hearty laugh when I took in the idea of your three hopeful sons being in the hospital at the one and same time. I suppose you think it is something that should not be laughed at. Well I agree with you on that point — it is not quite so funny as it might be. Low diet and doctor's medicines are not quite as agreeable as some things.

A truce to the blues and now for something lively. Our Corps has fallen back from Atlanta and is now holding a line along the Chattahoochee. The rest of the army I expect has gone on a grand flanking excursion, heading toward Macon. It is reported here today that the rebs have left Atlanta and gone after Sherman. I expect stirring things will happen in a day or two. General Slocum now commands our 6th Corps. 1st Lieut. P. H. Brookway (formerly Orderly Sergt. of Co. H.) now commands our Co. Capt. Delaney, as you are aware, is at home. There is very little of interest to write. I hope the chronic diarrhea will not get hold of James and Charles. It is a terrible disease. Love to all. Please send some stamps.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell
editorial:
Three brothers in three hospitals at the same time — and Alexander laughs. "Please excuse me, Mother, but I did have a hearty laugh when I took in the idea of your three hopeful sons being in the hospital at the one and same time." The dark humor of a veteran. "Low diet and doctor's medicines are not quite as agreeable as some things."

The military news is enormous: Sherman's army has swung south toward Macon in the "grand flanking excursion" that will force Hood to evacuate Atlanta. The 20th Corps holds the Chattahoochee line — and on September 2, they will march into the empty city. Alexander, in the hospital with scurvy, will miss the moment his corps has been fighting toward for four months.

author: alexander
notes: U.S. General Hospital, Chattanooga, Tenn. Sent from front with large number of sick and wounded on hospital train. **WHEELER'S RAID** — "We should have gone directly to Nashville, but old Wheeler had made a raid and torn up the road so we were obliged to stop here." Pretty sick yesterday and last night — much better today. Should be able to join regt. before a great while. **CHICAGO CONVENTION** — considerable anxiety about Presidential nominee. "We will know in a day or two." Nothing of interest to write.
transcription:
Sept. 2d, 1864
U. S. General Hospital
Chattanooga, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

The evening of the day I wrote you my last letter, I with a large number of other sick and wounded was put on board a hospital train and sent to this place. We were two nights and a day getting here. We should have gone directly to Nashville, but old Wheeler had made a raid and torn up the road so we were obliged to stop here. I do not know how long we shall remain here. Generally as soon as the men are able to hear it they send them on to Nashville. I was pretty sick yesterday and last night, but am very much better today. I shall be able to join the regt. before a great while, I think. Considerable anxiety is felt to know who the Presidential nominee is at the Chicago convention the 29th inst. We will know in a day or two. There is nothing of interest to write. Send your letters to the regt. as usual. Love to all.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell.
editorial: September 2, 1864 — the day Atlanta falls. Alexander is in a hospital in Chattanooga, moved there by hospital train because Wheeler's cavalry raiders tore up the Nashville railroad. He writes a brief, tired note about feeling sick and wondering who the Democrats will nominate in Chicago. He doesn't know that on this day, the city he shelled from 1¼ miles away, the city he saw from a ridge with its spires and chimneys, has been entered by his own 20th Corps. The campaign is over. He missed the ending.
sigSummary: Wheeler's cavalry tore up the Nashville road, so Alexander's hospital train, two nights and a day out, was forced to stop at Chattanooga, where he writes his mother a tired, brief note: pretty sick yesterday, much better today, soon able to rejoin the regiment. Even from a hospital bed he frets over the Chicago convention of the 29th, waiting a day or two to learn whom the Democrats will nominate for President.

transcription:
Sept. 18, 1864
U. S. Field Hospital No. 2
Chattanooga, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

Much to my gratification a day or two since the 60th N.Y. Vets. were sent to this place from the front to escort the Paymaster of the 20th Corps down, and of course they brought what mail there was for me at the Regt. (5 letters.) You can rest assured I was well pleased for I had not heard from you in a long, long, time, and I did not dare have the mail sent here for I was liable to be sent off to Nashville or some other place any time. Direct your letters to the regt. as usual. There is too much uncertainty to have them directed here. I am getting along pretty well, but how soon I shall be fit for duty I am unable to say. I may be well soon and it may take a long time to get this misnamed scurvy out of my blood. However I guess I will be all right before long. The man that gives out the medicine has just been around and given me a gay old drink of lime water — something very similar to lemonade. Then I say lime I don't mean lime such as they make mortar of, but limes, a fruit like lemons.

Luther is with the regt. He has been up to see me twice. A number of the boys have been up to see me. It is pleasant to have them here. The regt. is still here unless they have left this morning. I am sorry I shall not be able to draw pay with the regt. this time. Government owes me some two hundred and forty dollars. I may draw a little pay here, sufficient for my wants but no more.

What do the people of C. think of the draft. We all like it down here. There is no way to put down this rebellion but by force of arms. A few more vigorous pushes will shove them into the Atlantic Ocean.

When you speak in your letters of the tomatoes you are having, and the new potatoes, etc., etc. in such abundance, I long to be there to enjoy these good things with you, and I hope I shall before many months roll around. The letters I received from you were of Aug. 24th and 29th. The other letter was from Jack Ingram. I received six stamps in one of your letters which will do for some little time. I received the money and everything you sent except the tea, I think. Perhaps you did not put on enough postage for the tea. Tell Fannie I will try and write her before a great while. Love to all. Remember me to Mrs. B. If any body wants to know my political principles you tell them I am a "war man." That's enough. Please write often.

Your aff. Son,

Alex F. Hubbell

I am glad to see the copper heads don't like McClellan. It speaks well for him.
editorial:
"I am a 'war man.'" — Alexander's political identity has found its final form. Not Republican, not Democrat — a war man. The draft is good. Force of arms is the only way. And the postscript is pure Alexander: "I am glad to see the copper heads don't like McClellan. It speaks well for him." He still admires McClellan personally but defines himself by the war, not by party.

The lime water for scurvy — "I don't mean lime such as they make mortar of, but limes, a fruit like lemons" — is Alexander explaining the exotic to his mother in Champlain, New York. The same instinct that described Atlanta's spires from a ridge now describes a citrus fruit.

$240 owed by the government — nearly a year of a sergeant's pay. The army fights on credit.

Too uncertain of his next move to draw pay with the regiment, he reckoned the government owed him $240. His politics he stated plainly: "I am a 'war man.' That's enough."

location: In the field near Strasburg, Virginia
notes: In the field near Strasburg. **BATTLE NEAR WINCHESTER** — two days since, came out unhurt. **4 KILLED, 12 WOUNDED in Co.** James looking very well — nicely recruited. Day or two after Dr. Sweeney wrote, James rejoined regt. Still with Brigade Commissary — "getting fat, the result of good living." Have to walk on march but carry no load. Received letter with $2 and stamps. Also James rec'd 3 newspapers. **JAMES GOT CAPT. TO WRITE ALBANY** for state bounty — $25 — should have had it long since. Mother's investment in "2d hands" may well pay. **CAMPED NEAR BERRYVILLE** two weeks — reason James has not written. Lost good many men in fight two days since — whipped rebs, drove them to this place. **REGT. LOST 55 WOUNDED AND 10 KILLED.** Near Winchester — about 12 miles this side. (Written on back — note from Frances.)
transcription:
Sept. 21st, 1864
In the field near Strasburg

Dear Mother:

I sit down to write you a few lines, feeling very thankful that James came out of the battle near Winchester two days since unhurt. There were four killed and twelve wounded in our Co. James is looking very well, he got nicely recruited at the hospital. A day or two after Dr. Sweeney wrote James rejoined the regt. Dr. Sweeney is very kind to James and me, and some time since wished me to transfer him to you. I am still with the Brigade Commissary and am getting fat, the result of good living. I have to walk on the march but carry no load.

I rec'd your letter with the $2.00 and stamps, also James rec'd three newspapers with Mr. Hoyle's name on them. James got our Capt. to write to Albany for his state bounty which is twenty-five dollars and ordered it sent to you. He should have had it long since. The letter was sent a few days since. I think the money you invested in the "2d hands" may well pay. It may be well to invest some of our money in the capital of the C. Bank, but will leave you to do as you think best.

We were camped near Berryville two weeks and while there our Regt. drilled twice a day, leaving hardly time to cook. That is the reason James has not written. We lost a good many men in the fight two days since, but whipped the rebs and drove them to this place where they are making a stand, but they will soon have to leave. Our regt. lost 55 wounded and 10 killed. We are now about twelve miles this side of Winchester. Am glad to hear that you and Frances are well. We are pleased to hear from you so often, hope that you will continue to write often.

From your aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell

(Written on back of this letter — a note from Frances.)
editorial:
Third Winchester — Sheridan's first great victory in the Shenandoah Valley. The 153rd NY lost 65 men (55 wounded, 10 killed) — and James, just back from the hospital at Frederick, came through unhurt. Charles, at the Brigade Commissary, is "getting fat" while his regiment bleeds. The irony is not lost, but Charles doesn't dwell on it.

The rebs are "making a stand" at Strasburg — Fisher's Hill. Sheridan will attack the next day (September 22) and rout them again. Charles doesn't know it yet, but he's describing the setup for another victory.

transcription:
September 21, 1864
U. S. Hospital No. 2
Chattanooga, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

Have you taken a realizing sense that I have now been in the U. S. Service as a soldier three years — three long — long — weary years! Yes — three years ago today I took an oath to serve the United States of America faithfully as a soldier for the term of "three years or the war," and I can conscientiously say that I have with God's help done my best to bear that oath and do my duty as a soldier should do. And now, dear Mother, I want you to join me, (and I know you will) in thanking God for his kind and watchful care over me in preserving me through so many dangers and temptations to which I have been exposed in the past terrible three years of war, and to ask a continuance of his kind care over me during the remainder of my term of service.

When I think of all the things which I have passed my heart is too full to speak. This is the first time since I have been in the service that I have been in a general hospital sick. You know I was in one last fall but then I was wounded and was only a short time from the regt.

Well, I wrote you, only a day or two since, and have nothing of special interest to communicate. I am getting along very well, I think. There is one very singular thing about it — as soon as it is night comes I am as blind as a bat. However it may wear off in time. There are a number here troubled in the same way. Direct your letters to the regt. Give my regards to Mrs. B. Love to all,

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell.

P.S. The morning papers give an acct. of a heavy fight in the Shenandoah Valley. I am very anxious to hear from the boys.
editorial:
September 21, 1864 — three years to the day since Alexander took his oath. "Three long — long — weary years!" The dashes are Alexander's breathing. "My heart is too full to speak." This is the closest Alexander comes to breaking down on paper.

The night blindness is grimly specific — a symptom of severe vitamin A deficiency, which accompanies scurvy. "As blind as a bat" every night, with "a number here troubled in the same way." The Atlanta Campaign didn't just exhaust these men — it blinded them.

The postscript is its own drama: "The morning papers give an acct. of a heavy fight in the Shenandoah Valley." Alexander reads about Third Winchester in a Chattanooga hospital. His brothers were in it. He doesn't know if they're alive. On the same day, Charles writes from Strasburg to say James came through unhurt. The letters will cross in the mail.
sigSummary: Three years to the day since he swore his oath, Alexander writes from U.S. Hospital No. 2 in Chattanooga — "three long — long — weary years!" — his first time hospitalized sick rather than wounded. He reports a strange affliction: "as soon as it is night comes I am as blind as a bat," with others around him troubled the same way. A postscript betrays his dread: morning papers carry word of a heavy fight in the Shenandoah Valley, and he is anxious to hear from the boys.

author: james
notes: Harrisonburg, Shenandoah Valley. Started Oct 4, continued Oct 12. **TWO FIGHTS — driving rebels both times.** Last pursuit — inhabitants said rebs went through "with a rush," army demoralized. Passed several burning wagons in night pursuit. "You have travelled this road once, I think." **OCT 12 — FALLEN BACK TO CEDAR CREEK NEAR STRASBURG.** Burning barns and forage as they went. **ALEX DOUGLAS MISSING — GUERRILLAS.** Fell to rear with one man — not seen or heard of since. Boys running through houses taking what they choose — "exasperates the rebels very much." "This other fellow from our company was one of the greatest house thieves in our regt." "Ma, there is a Yankee down cellar taking all our preserves and bacon." "Ma, see that Yankee looking in the oven." Little boy of brigade gobbled while foraging — shot up with rebel deserters — slipped out during fight. **LETTER FROM HOME** — Mother says Alex quite ill. "I have seen one month in the hospital since I enlisted." Charley's health now pretty good. Some talk about going to Louisiana. **ELECTION** — "I'm a voter; I go for old Abe; he is the man." Little Mac will probably run strong. War lasted nearly four years — "I would like to see it ended."
transcription:
October 4, 1864
Harrisonburg
In the Shenandoah Valley

Dear Alex:

When did I write you last! I know it is a long time since. Do not think because I have not written you that I have forgotten you. We have had two fights of which you have undoubtedly heard, driving the rebels both times. The last pursuit the inhabitants of the towns through which we passed said the Rebs went through there with a rush, and that their army was demoralized. In the road in the pursuit during the night we passed several of their wagons burning. I do not believe that the Johnnies will make another stand here in the valley. You have travelled this road once, I think.

October 12th — Since I commenced this we have fallen back to Cedar Creek near Strasburg — burning barns and forage as we went. Alex Douglas has been boggled by the guerrillas, it is thought. He fell to the rear several days since with one man of our company while on a march and has not been seen or heard of since. The boys in this army have a habit of running through the houses and taking whatever they choose, which I think exasperates the rebels very much, and I cannot but fear for a straggler. This other fellow from our company was one of the greatest house thieves in our regt. Douglas was not any of that. I have heard this thief tell some of his stories. While he was in one house one of the children said, "Ma, there is a Yankee down cellar taking all our preserves and bacon." "Ma, see that Yankee looking in the oven." If they remonstrated with him he would "blackguard" them. I do not pity this fellow much. This running through houses is checked carefully by the officers but cannot always be prevented. Sometime before the battle of Winchester there was a little boy of our brigade gobbled while foraging. He was shot up with rebel deserters. During the fight they were ordered to turn out and help fight; he slipped out with them and made his escape. He said they were going to hang him for a spy.

Last night I received a letter from home. They want to know why we do not write. I have been rather negligent in writing. Charley has written several times but they have not received his letters; the mails have been irregular. Mother says you are quite ill. I hope you are better ere this. I have seen one month in the hospital since I enlisted. I'm all right now. Charley's health is now pretty good. There is some talk about our going to Louisiana. I hope we will not. I do not like the climate.

What are your views on the coming elections? I'm a voter; I go for old Abe; he is the man, I think. Little Mac will probably run strong. This war has lasted nearly four years. I would like to see it ended, and believe it will be soon.

Your aff. brother

James
editorial:
James's Shenandoah letter is the youngest brother's most substantial war narrative. The foraging stories are priceless — "Ma, there is a Yankee down cellar taking all our preserves and bacon." "Ma, see that Yankee looking in the oven." James tells these with a storyteller's ear, but then pivots to the consequences: Alex Douglas is missing, probably captured by guerrillas. "I cannot but fear for a straggler." The "house thief" from his company may be dead for his thieving.

The captured boy who was nearly hanged as a spy — "He said they were going to hang him for a spy" — is another James detail. The war at the individual level: a boy foraging, grabbed by rebel deserters, nearly executed, escaping in the confusion of battle.

"I'm a voter; I go for old Abe; he is the man." James at 18 (or 19) votes Lincoln without Alexander's agonizing. The youngest brother's politics are the simplest.

He fears Alex Douglas, fallen to the rear on a march, has been "boggled by the guerrillas," and recounts a foraging boy nearly hanged as a spy who slipped free mid-battle. At 18 he votes plainly: "I go for old Abe; he is the man."

notes: Harrisonburg, Shenandoah Valley. **REJOINED REGT. last day of Sept.** Too many clerks in commissary — told to go back. Quite fat and in good health. James very well. No gun yet — turned in gun when left regt. **RECRUIT FROM FRESSEVILLE — $1,202 BOUNTY.** Enlisted one year. About 90 miles from Harper's Ferry. **CAVALRY BURNED BARNS AND GRIST MILLS** as far as Stanton (Staunton). Advanced 8 miles for flour, came back. Troops suffered from want of rations — wagoned from Harper's Ferry. On march, foraged: "pigs, sheep, chickens, apples, butter, etc." Provost Marshall can't stop it. Rich valley — fine farming country. Many wounded rebs in hospital. Recruits coming fast. **BURNED ALL FENCES** — oak rails make good fire. Water and wood scarce. Soldiers daily duty: "cook, clean his gun and look over his clothes and pick off the vermin." **"A man is no soldier unless he is lousy."** Some think going to Louisiana. $75 from Albany — James's state bounty?
transcription:
Oct. 4, 1864
Harrisonburg

As the mail leaves soon I will write a few lines. I rejoined the regt. the last day of Sept. There were too many clerks there in the commissary so they told two of us to go to our regts. I am quite fat and am in good health. James is very well. I have no gun yet, as I turned in my gun when I left the regt. Expect to have one soon.

A few days since a recruit from Fresseville came to our Co. He rec'd. $1202 bounty. Enlisted for one year. We have been here three days. I don't know which way we will move from here. Have chased the rebs a long way. It is about ninety miles from here to Harper's Ferry. The cavalry have been as far as Stanton and have burned barns and grist mills. We advanced to the next town about 8 miles from here where we got a lot of flour and came back here the next day. The troops have suffered some from want of rations. Rations are wagoned here from Harper's Ferry. On the march the troops we foraged a great deal. Pigs, sheep, chickens, apples, butter, etc. There is a Provost Marshall to stop such doings but it is done for all that. This is a rich valley — a fine farming country. There are a great many wounded rebs in the hospital here. We have also passed other towns where the rebs were in hospitals. They were sent this way after the fight near Bunker Hill.

Recruits are coming to this army fast. Quite a number have joined our regt. We have burned all the fences for a long ways around this place except where there is a safe guard. These oak rails make a good fire. This is a bad place to camp as water and wood are scarce. Have to go quite a distance for them. Do you know a soldier's daily duty? It is to cook, clean his gun and look over his clothes and pick off the vermin. On a march the soldiers get pretty lousy as they have no kettles to heat water to boil their clothes. It is a common saying that a man is no soldier unless he is lousy. Some of the men think that we are going to Louisiana to spend the winter. I hope not.

Have you rec'd seventy-five dollars from Albany — James' state bounty? James rec'd two or three days since two democratic newspapers (Journal of Commerce). We expect to receive a letter from you next mail. It is some time since we received one.

Charles
editorial:
Charles's Shenandoah description is pure quartermaster's eye: $1,202 bounties, rations wagoned 90 miles, fences burned for fuel, foraging despite the Provost Marshall. "Pigs, sheep, chickens, apples, butter, etc." — the inventory of a rich valley being consumed by an army.

"Do you know a soldier's daily duty? It is to cook, clean his gun and look over his clothes and pick off the vermin." This is Charles at his most characteristic — the practical observer who describes war as housekeeping. "A man is no soldier unless he is lousy." Alexander would never write that sentence, but Charles can, because Charles sees the army as work, not drama.
sigSummary: Charles writes to Alexander from Harrisonburg, fresh off rejoining the regiment after being cut loose from a too-crowded commissary, and the war reaches him as ledger and labor: a Fresseville recruit drawing $1,202 bounty for one year, rations wagoned ninety miles from Harper's Ferry, cavalry burning barns and grist mills toward Stanton. "A man is no soldier unless he is lousy," he reports — war as housekeeping in a rich valley being eaten bare.

transcription:
Oct. 22, 1864
Camp near Strasburg, Va.

Dear Mother:

James and I rec'd a lot of newspapers Oct. 18th and were anticipating a good deal of pleasure next day in reading them. Well, next morning I was awakened by a sharp volley of musketry. James exclaimed, "The Rebs are here!" We jumped up and put on our accoutrements and fell in behind our breastworks, but in a few minutes were ordered to pack up. We took our tents down in a jiffy. By that time the rebs were close to us. It was a surprise attack. They got behind our breastworks before we knew it. Our Brigade was ordered to leave our breastworks and form on the other side of a deep ravine. We jumped over the breastworks very quick as the Rebs were firing into us and we were moving up the hill the bullets came very thick. A good many of our men were shot here. James was wounded near this place. A Sergeant of our Co. says that as he was going to the rear with a wounded man he saw James; that James rec'd. a flesh wound in the thigh or hip and walked about five miles to the hospital. Says James had made a bandage of his drawers. He went with James to the hospital and says James is all right. James Lucas was reported killed, but I have since learned that he was taken to the hospital shot through the head and arm. Sergeant Pelkier (pronounced Pelky) from Corbeau of our town was shot through the leg. Alex Douglas has been missing about ten or twelve days. While on the march here, he and another man of our Co. were either captured or killed. It is supposed that they got to the rear and were taken prisoners by guerillas. Every one is very sorry about Douglas as he was very much liked. He and the other man were mounted. James Lucas wrote Mr. Douglas about Alex. Lieut. Col. Strain was wounded in the arm in the fight on the 19th of Oct. Our Regt. had about 50 wounded and 8 killed. Our Co. had 7 wounded and 2 killed.

The Rebs drove us out of our camp in the morning when we lost a great many men, but we rallied and drove them, recapturing all our artillery and all of theirs. We drove them out of our camp and beyond to Fisher's Hill. The Rebs came into our camp by the flank where the 8th Corps lay. I am very thankful that I did not get scratched. I think that I have received all your letters but am sorry that you have not received mine. I wrote two from Harrisburg. Am very sorry about Lucas. He rec'd a letter from home the night before the fight and intended to write the next day. Did you receive a letter from Dr. Sweeney some time since? He inquired of me if you did. Please write soon and send me a few stamps.

From your aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell
editorial:
"James exclaimed, 'The Rebs are here!'" — the Battle of Cedar Creek begins in the Hubbell tent with a shout. Charles tells the story of surprise and chaos: breastworks overrun, brigade ordered across a ravine, bullets thick on the hill, James hit. The bandage made from drawers — the youngest brother's first wound, improvised from underwear.

Cedar Creek was Early's last great gamble — a dawn surprise attack that rolled up the Union left (the 8th Corps) and drove Sheridan's army from its camp. Then Sheridan rode from Winchester ("Sheridan's Ride" — the famous poem) and rallied the troops for a crushing counterattack. Charles tells none of the famous story — no Sheridan, no ride, no poetry. He tells the soldier's story: "We jumped up and put on our accoutrements." "The bullets came very thick." "I am very thankful that I did not get scratched."

The casualty list is the Hubbell family's worst day: James wounded, Lucas shot through the head, Pelky through the leg, Douglas still missing, Strain's arm, 7 wounded and 2 killed in the company alone. And the newspapers from October 18 that James and Charles were looking forward to reading — never read.
sigSummary: At dawn near Strasburg, James woke Charles with a shout — "The Rebs are here!" — and the Battle of Cedar Creek erupted. Charles tells a soldier's story of surprise: breastworks overrun, his brigade scrambling across a ravine as bullets came thick up the hill. James took a flesh wound to the hip and walked five miles to the hospital, a bandage torn from his own drawers. 7 wounded, 2 killed in his company alone.

notes: U.S.A. Hospital No. 3, Nashville, Tenn. "You can have no idea how anxious I am to hear from you all." Wants letter directed here. **WOULD NOT TAKE OATH** prescribed in NY voting law — "have consequently lost my chance of voting." **"COULD I HAVE VOTED I SHOULD HAVE CAST IT 'SQUARE AND FAIR' FOR ABRAHAM LINCOLN."** "The majority of soldiers will vote that way." Ten (perhaps more) days longer.
transcription:
October 26th, 1864
U.S.A. Hospital No. 3
Nashville, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

You can have no idea how anxious I am to hear from you all and I have at length determined to have a letter directed here. So please, immediately on receipt of this, write me a long letter telling me all the news since last August — the date of the last letter I received from you, and do not fail to send it by return mail. I think I shall be here ten (and perhaps more) days longer.

I would not take the oath prescribed in the New York voting law and have consequently lost my chance of voting. Could I have voted I should have cast it "square and fair" for Abraham Lincoln. The majority of soldiers will vote that way.

Direct your letter simply to Nashville, Tenn. In case I am not here when it arrives I can write to Postmaster and have it sent on.

Love to all.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell
editorial:
"Could I have voted I should have cast it 'square and fair' for Abraham Lincoln." The political journey that began with "my heart still yearns" for McClellan in April is over. Alexander Hubbell, the man who admired McClellan's generalship and the Democratic convention's "right spirit," will not vote — but if he could, it would be for Lincoln.

The NY voting oath he refused is a footnote to a larger story: a man who will fight but won't swear on someone else's terms. The oath of September 21, 1861 — "three years or the war" — was enough. He doesn't need another one.
sigSummary: Alexander writes from U.S.A. Hospital No. 3 in Nashville that he refused the oath prescribed in New York's voting law and so lost his chance to vote — yet "could I have voted I should have cast it 'square and fair' for Abraham Lincoln," adding that the majority of soldiers will vote that way. Beneath the politics runs a quieter ache: a son begging his mother to write "a long letter telling me all the news since last August."

transcription:
October 29th, 1864
Patterson Park Hospital
Baltimore, Md.

Dear Alex:

I had a letter written and sealed which I carried in my pocket for a long time. I have now determined to add another before I send it to you. I was wounded in the left thigh at Cedar Run. It is nothing but a flesh wound and is doing well. I walked several miles after being hit in order not to fall into the Johnnies hands. They were then driving our forces, but things changed before night. Our forces were driving them full well. Their army was completely demoralized. They threw away everything. We got their wagon train, artillery and almost everything they had. The Johnnies attacked and routed the eighth Corps before daylight. This rather took our force by surprise and compelled them to retreat as they were flanked and the breastworks would be of no use. I do not believe the Rebs will try it again in the Valley — three times terribly whipped.

Our Co. was very much cut up. It was also badly cut up at Winchester, so that there is scarcely anything left of it. Lucas was badly wounded. He is the only one you know in the company. Three fellows assisted me to the hospital which was situated in a barn several miles back. I had gone part of the way myself, but was about played out when they came along. I remained at the Hospital a day and was then sent on here. I had thirty miles to ride in an army wagon to get to a railroad station, and then one hundred and twenty in a freight car. That journey was a hard one.

The hospital here is a very comfortable one and the fare very good. Baltimore seems to be the first great place to which our wounded and sick are sent. They are transferred from here to Philadelphia. You were right when I heard from you last. I hope you have got well ere this. I look for a speedy termination of the war. I think we shall be able to judge a good deal come morning it is after the Presidential election. I shall be able to vote here and shall cast my vote for Abraham Lincoln. I hope he will be elected.

We have not been paid for six months. I think it is about time for the Paymaster to visit us. I do not know how long I will be here but will send you my address; it is Patterson Park Hospital, Baltimore, M.D.

Your affectionate Brother,

James.
editorial:
James's Cedar Creek is told by a wounded man who walked for miles to avoid capture, then rode thirty miles in an army wagon and 120 in a freight car. "That journey was a hard one." The understatement of a teenager who has been shot, walked on it, and ridden 150 miles to a hospital.

"I do not believe the Rebs will try it again in the Valley — three times terribly whipped." James counts the victories: Winchester, Fisher's Hill, Cedar Creek. The Shenandoah is done. At 18 or 19, he analyzes the campaign like a veteran.

"I shall be able to vote here and shall cast my vote for Abraham Lincoln." All three Hubbell brothers — Alexander in Nashville, James in Baltimore, Charles in the Shenandoah — will vote or would vote for Lincoln. The family that was pro-McClellan in April is Lincoln by November.

transcription:
Nov. 4, 1864
Camp at Cedar Creek, Va.

Dear Mother:

I read your letter announcing grandmothers death two days since. Was not surprised as she was so old. I suppose Aunt Mary will come North if she can get away.

Have not heard from James nor any of our wounded in the last fight. Two of our Co. who saw him say that his wound is not dangerous. Our Chaplain saw him in the hospital sitting up in bed. He told me James was doing well. I asked the Chaplain if his wound was serious. He said he did not know. I told him that James walked to the hospital. He then said it must be a flesh wound. Our Chaplain is none home sick. The badly wounded were at the hospital at Winchester. The others are forwarded on to the other hospitals. James Lucas, I heard, lay on the ground all day till he was taken up by an ambulance. I did not see him. However that I ought to write his folks, but if you will tell them that he was shot then he head and an arm it will do as well. Our Chaplain told me that he probably would not recover. I do not whether James is at Winchester or been sent on to some other city. The morning of the fight there were no ambulances and if a man could not walk he had to lay on the ground unless some of the soldiers carried him. Segt. Pelkier, of our town, shot in the leg, was carried by some of our Co. & left in a barn to be made prisoner of by the rebs as was supposed, but when we came back that night he was there.

We now drill & have dress parade, regular camp life. Do not know how long we will stay here, but think not long. De Sweeney was taken prisoner the morning of the fight, but got away from the rebs that night. I do not know how long we will stay here, but think not long. De Sweeney was taken prisoner the morning of the fight, but got away from the rebs that night. Did not know what had become of James until that night after dark.

Sunday, 6th: This morning we were called up at 4 oclock & fell into line with our arms. It looked as if they expected an attack, but after standing till daylight we broke ranks & cooked our breakfast. After eating we had Brigade Review & inspection.

I sent my vote to Silas, voted for Lincoln. Only two votes for Lincoln in our Co.

(Remainder of letter missing) From,

C. F. Hubbell (Charles)
editorial:
"Only two votes for Lincoln in our Co." — Charles is one of two Lincoln men in a McClellan company. The 153rd NY's company is exactly the border-state/Irish constituency Alexander described: soldiers who fight for the Union but vote against Lincoln. Charles votes his conscience and counts himself in the minority.

The company has 22 men left. Two fights in the Shenandoah — 23 killed and wounded. The math is brutal: the company is nearly destroyed. "In the fight bullets flew all around me but I came out without a scratch." Charles's survival is statistical improbability.

"The morning of the fight there were no ambulances and if a man could not walk he had to lay on the ground unless some of the soldiers carried him." Cedar Creek's medical reality: wounded men on the ground with no help coming.
sigSummary: Grandmother's death reaches Charles in camp at Cedar Creek, where his company is down to its survivors. He hunts for news of the wounded: brother James walked to the hospital, likely a flesh wound; James Lucas lay on the ground all day before an ambulance came; Sgt. Pelkier, shot in the leg, was left in a barn for the rebels but found alive that night. "I sent my vote to Silas, voted for Lincoln. Only two votes for Lincoln in our Co."
